thread.title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 37: How Warren Buffett's True Secret To Success Can Make You Rich

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 37: How Warren Buffett's True Secret To Success Can Make You Rich
text:
(Source: imgflip )
Introduction First, let me be very clear that this is my personal portfolio tailored to my specific financial situation, risk profile, time horizon, and personality traits. I am not recommending anyone mirror this portfolio, which is merely designed to show my unique, rule-based, methodical approach to value-focused, long-term, dividend growth investing.
My situation is unique, as though only 31, I'm already retired (medical retirement from the Army), thus making this portfolio an income-focused retirement one (though in a taxable account). I'm also working full-time (self-employed), and thus have an external source of income to continually add to this portfolio. I do not plan to actually tap the portfolio's income stream for 20-25 years, when I plan to move my family (and help support my parents) to the promised land of my people (retired dividend investors): Sarasota, Florida.
What this portfolio can be used for is investing ideas; however, this portfolio includes high-, low-, as well as medium-risk stocks, so it's up to each individual to do their own individual research and decide which, if any, of my holdings are right for you.
For a detailed explanation of my methodology, please read my introductory article to the EDDGE (Eternal Daily Dividend Growth Experiment) 4.0 portfolio. However, keep in mind that the portfolio is not static, and both it and the underlying investment strategy will evolve and adapt over time. This is because a changing world, new knowledge, and more experience will cause me to fine-tune it over coming years and decades to maximize my income and total returns.
The reason behind owning such a widely diversified portfolio is because I've built this strategy using historical statistical analysis. Statistics requires large sample sizes to have any useful predictive power, and so, the more stocks I own, the more likely the long-term total returns are to approximate the projected returns. As a side benefit, it also creates a highly stable "bunker" portfolio that is likely to easily survive whatever future market storm might come. It also creates a stream of near-daily dividends which will allow me to compound my dividend reinvestment faster.
Note that this experiment has to hit certain performance targets within a fixed time frame:
Break even within 3 years (Kevin O'Leary Principle: If you don't make money after 3 years, it's a hobby, not a business".) Match the market within 4 years. Beat the market within 5 years (on an unlevered basis). Beat smart beta ETFs that have historically outperformed the S&P 500 (like NOBL ) within 6 years. Beat all ETFs or smart beta ETFs (like QQQ ) within 7 years. In case the portfolio fails to hit these targets, then I'll adapt it to add what is outperforming it. That means switching to an alternative plan, which tentatively looks like this:
25% QQQ (Nasdaq ETF, which I consider a superior index to the S&P 500) 25% SCHD (Dividend achiever ETF, which is also superior to the S&P 500) 10% non-dividend stocks (such as Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), and Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A , BRK.B )) 40% individual dividend growth stocks (focused on maximizing long-term total return potential via 20-25 stocks) Also, to make it easier to digest, I've decided to try separating my weekly investment lesson/commentary from the actual portfolio update. This week's commentary explains why rising oil prices aren't likely to crash either the economy or the stock market and might even make you rich.
Behold The Secret To Buffett's Success Warren Buffett is the world's most famous value investor and for good reason. Between 1965 and 2017, Berkshire Hathaway managed to compound shareholder wealth at an astonishing 20.8% CAGR. In comparison, the S&P 500 returned a still impressive 9.7%. That double-digit outperformance for 52 years meant that $10,000 invested in Berkshire and the S&P 500 in 1965 would have turned into $197 million and $1.28 million respectively. Or to put another way, Buffett beat the market by 155 times over the past half century.
Wouldn't it be great if you could copy Buffett's strategy? You might not be able to match his returns exactly, but if you could come even close, the results might be spectacular over time. Well, a team of researchers actually did a detailed analytical study of Buffett's methods.
In "Buffett's Alpha" , three researchers from Columbia University and New York University found that there were four main factors to Buffett's stunning success over the decades:
Value: Buffett has a tendency to favor low price-to-book value stocks. Safe: He bets against beta via low volatility stocks. Quality: he favors quality companies (profitable, growing) over lower quality distressed firms (such as dividend growth stocks). Leverage: Between 1976 and 2011 (when study looked at), Buffett averaged 1.6 times leverage via Berkshire's use of insurance float. Now, to any student of market history (or my long-term readers), this doesn't come as a surprise. That's because what Buffett was doing is called alpha factor investing. That means he was one of the first to determine that using certain strategies could help achieve market beating returns over time.
Historical studies have found there are five major alpha factors :
size (small and medium caps) value (undervalued stocks low volatility (low beta) dividend growth stocks (such as dividend aristocrats and kings, a proxy for quality) equal weighting (as opposed to market weighting as most index funds do) So, does this mean that using alpha factors (also called factor tilt or smart beta investing) can make us all into the next Warren Buffett?
Actually no. Because while Buffett's use of factor tilt investing and leverage is certainly replicable, the most important part of his "secret sauce" isn't.
Buffett's True Super Power Is Discipline And The Patience Of A Saint
(Source: Slideplayer )
Buffett's true super power isn't just knowing what strategies work best over time. Rather his incredible emotional control allows him to put those strategies into practice via long-term patience and a dedication to buy and hold investing that requires an iron stomach to ride out the market's worst crashes.
(Source: Berkshire Hathaway Annual Letter )
For example, take a look at the four worst periods of underperformance for Berkshire stock. Some of you might remember that Buffett was mocked for being "washed up" in the tech boom because Berkshire got cut in half while tech stocks soared. That was due to the market's irrational mania and the adoption of a "value investing is dead, tech can only go up!" mindset.
However, that was hardly the only time that Buffett underperformed and by a lot. In the 1970s, Buffett and his investors had to endure an epic three year 59% crash. But guess what? It was during this major bear market that Buffett was snapping up great investments at fire sale prices which is what largely accounted for the man's legendary future gains.
This means that Buffett's true super power is actually composed of two parts. First, the ability to think like a contrarian, which isn't something you're born with but have to develop over time (patience, discipline, practice).
But guess what? Just as important to Buffett's success is the patience of a saint and the ability to ignore the haters and doubters. As Buffett recently said, share prices over even several years don't determine whether or not you've made a good investment. " You're right because your facts and reasoning are right ."
In other words, Buffett's true super power is knowing what works, and having the confidence and patience to invest the smart way for as long as it takes for the market to catch up to the facts.
(Source: Ploutos)
Because even the smartest investors using the best strategies can underperform for long stretches. Take those alpha factors for example. While over the long-term (10+ years) they all beat the market, various investing styles do better at different times based on where we are in the market cycle.
(Source: Ploutos)
For example, over the last five years, low volatility has lost to the market. That makes sense since during the second longest bull market growth stocks have been all the rage.
That's the same reason that value stocks have underperformed during the past three years. However, note that if you wait long enough? Well, then, these market beating strategies (many which Buffet has made a fortune using) will indeed make your rich over time.
(Source: Ploutos)
And in case you think that the above data is cherry picking and that investors can't actually invest based on these strategies, here are five ETFs that have proven that factor investing works. Note that some are relatively new and none perfectly track their benchmarks. But over time you can see that they get close and the alpha they deliver over the market is real and significant.
But just remember that no strategy is going to beat the market all of the time. If it did, everyone in the world would adopt it, and those stocks would become overpriced and the strategy would stop working. The fact that the best strategies over time drift in and out of favor is the very reason that patient, disciplined, and smart investors can beat the market over time and achieve our financial dreams.
The key is to diversify out portfolios not just by holdings (or through ETFs) but by strategies themselves. That way something is always beating the market for us and more importantly giving us the confidence to stick to the optimal long-term plan for each of us .
The State Of The Economy (aka Recession Watch) I use five key meta analyses to track the health of the economy. That includes those which have historically proven to be good predictors of recessions: the yield curve, the BaR economic graph, Jeff Miller's meta analysis of leading economic indicators, the St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator, and the New York Fed's real-time GDP growth tracker.
(Source: Business Insider )
The yield curve has proven the single-most accurate predictor of recessions over the past 80 years. Specifically, when the curve inverts, or goes below 0 (because short-term rates rise above long-term rates), then a recession becomes highly likely. It usually begins within 12-18 months.

Current 2/10 Yield Curve: 0.42% (down from 0.48% last week)
A few weeks ago, the curve fell as low as 0.41%, the lowest number since 2007. In the past week, the market's freakout over Italian politics and concerns over tariffs caused a major rally in bonds that resulted in significant yield curve compression. Fortunately, history shows that the actual number isn't significant, and recession risk is low as long as the curve is positive .
Overall, I'm still optimistic that strong economic growth and rising inflation expectations should help to keep long-term rates rising over time and thus put off any potential inversion for many months, if not years. That's especially true if the Federal Reserve avoids hiking short-term rates too aggressively if the curve falls too low.
The second economic indicator I watch is Economic PI's baseline and rate of change, or BaR economic analysis grid. This is another meta analysis incorporating 19 leading indicators that track every aspect of the US economy. That includes the yield curve, through a different version of it.
(Source: Economic PI )
The BaR grid has shown to be a reliable indicator predicting the 1980, 1990, 2001, and 2007 recessions.
With 10 out of 19 economic indicators in the expansion quadrant (indicating accelerating growth), and 9 out of 19 still showing positive (though decelerating) growth, there remains little cause for concern.
(Source: Economic PI)
Note that seven weeks ago, there were 12 economic indicators in the expansion quadrant, so the trend is still slightly negative but not statistically significant. In fact, the mean coordinate point (economic aggregate) remains at a neutral position but about 36% above baseline. That's about the same level as last week.
Next, there's Jeff Miller's excellent economic indicator snapshot, a rich source of numerous useful market/economic data. It also provides an actual percentage probability estimate for how likely a recession is to start in the next few months.
(Source: Jeff Miller )
What I'm looking at here is the quantitative estimates of short-term recession risks. In this case, the four-month recession risk is about 1.09%, while the probability of a recession starting within nine months is about 24%. While that is up slightly from last quarter, I don't consider it statistically significant. However, I will be watching inflation expectations closely (which drive bond yields) to see if the bond market loses confidence in the country's long-term growth prospects.
For another look at recession risk, I like to use the St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator. This looks at the risk of a recession beginning in the current month (it's actually delayed two months). It uses a four-month running average of leading economic indicators.
(Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve )
The way to read this graph is to understand that in the past (since 1967), as long as the reading (currently 0.16% recession risk) is under 18%, the economy has never been in a recession. This means that this graph can tell us with about a two-month lead time whether or not the economy is likely to be contracting.
Current Economic Growth Projections Ok, so the economy is nowhere close to a recession right now. But how fast is it growing? Well, we have two models for that, courtesy of the Atlanta Fed and New York Fed .
(Source: Atlanta Federal Reserve)
(Source: New York Federal Reserve)
Note that these are just models and depending on how they weight different leading indicators the projections can be wildly different. But they can offer us a reasonable estimate of current economic growth (range of 3.3% to 4.8%). More importantly, the projection trends have remained positive all quarter indicating that US economic growth appears to be not just strong but getting stronger over the last few months.
That bodes well for continued job growth, and thus, a continued tightening of the labor market that should eventually boost wages at a faster rate. Last month, private sector wages grew 2.9% YOY, which is up from 2.6% a year ago. Meanwhile, the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates that wage growth is now 2.7% YOY and 2.8% for non-supervisory positions (80% of workers).
That, in turn, could spur stronger consumer spending (70% of the US economy) and drive stronger corporate investment and earnings/cash flow/dividend growth. In fact, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, consumer spending in the last two months grew at 0.5% and 0.6% month over month, respectively.
Master Watchlist There are about 3,000 dividend-paying stocks in America (including special dividends and variable payers). This list has a goal of eventually listing all low-/medium-risk dividend growth stocks that have the potential to achieve 10+% total return potential.
Target yield indicates approximately fair value, which is the most I'd ever recommending paying for a company, no matter how good it is.
Total return potential is taken from the Gordon Dividend Growth model, which found that over time, total return for dividend stocks tracks yield + long-term dividend growth (a proxy for earnings and cash flow growth).
The projected dividend growth is from either management guidance or the current analyst consensus. Finally, I've included a sector column because some investors, for various reasons, don't want to/can't invest in MLPs.
Bolded and bracketed stocks are at fair value or better and worth buying today. The order of the stocks is the order I recommend buying them in, assuming that maximizing total return is your primary goal.

Buys/Sells This Week Bought $500 Spectra Energy ( SEP ) Bought $500 Silicon Motion Technology Corp. ( SIMO ) Bought $1850 EQT Midstream Partners ( EQM ) Silicon Motion was the new stock of the week, and my third tech company. Spectra Energy Partners is actually an arbitrage opportunity. It's being acquired by Enbridge Inc. ( ENB ) which is the best low risk, high-yield income growth investment opportunity since the financial crisis.
Owners of Spectra will be getting 1.01 shares of ENB per unit of Spectra which is actually trading about 2% cheaper. This creates a chance to pick up Enbridge shares at a 3% discount or the equivalent of about $29.70. That's a yield of 6.8% and just seven times forward cash flow. It's very rare to get the chance to pick up a high-yield blue chip stock that's becoming a dividend aristocrat in 2020 (and growing at 10% per year) for such an insanely low valuation.
EQM was an unexpected opportunity to double down and drastically lower the cost basis on one of the top ranked stocks on my master watchlist. Its coverage ratio is rock solid at 1.4, and management plans to grow the distribution by 15% to 20% for the next few years with no equity issuance needed through the end of 2020. Leverage ratio is 1.82, and management plans to cap it at 3.5 over the long-term (industry average 4.4, max safe level 5.0).
Plan For The Next Week This week's new stock is InterDigital, the second highest ranked company on my master watchlist. InterDigital is a fast growing telecom radio manufacturer that owns 19,000 patents. it is poised to make a killing off the switch to 5G and the coming revolutions in the internet of things, and driverless cars.
Over the past 5 years, IDCC has grown its dividend 27% annually and analysts are forecasting 25% annual earnings growth over the next decade. If IDCC can grow its payout anywhere close to that, it's very likely to crush the market. Best of all, it's currently about 16% undervalued.
I'm also going to be doubling down yet again on Spectra Energy/Enbridge (soon to be the same company). I'll be lowering my cost basis in Spectra as a way to earn a 3% discount on ENB shares. When the merger goes through (likely next three to six months), Enbridge will be my biggest holding (about 4.6% of portfolio) and my cost basis will be much lower than when I started.
Enbridge is the Berkshire of midstream, and I consider it the fattest pitch of the last 10 years. So, I'll keep doubling down on my highest conviction low risk, high-yield income growth opportunity for as long as the market wants to remain stupid and give me the opportunity.

Over time, as I diversify my portfolio, the yield will fall to about 3-4%. But the dividend growth rate should rise to about 9-10%. Ultimately, the goal is to build a highly diversified, low-risk, high-yielding portfolio with strong enough dividend growth to achieve 10-11% inflation-adjusted total returns.
For perspective, the S&P 500's 20-year median annual dividend growth rate has been 6.2% . So, the goal is to about double the market's yield, with about 3-4% faster dividend growth. Since 1871, the S&P 500 has generated annual total returns of 9.1% . The market's historical inflation adjusted total return has been 7.0%.
Thus, the idea is to prove that a high-yield dividend growth portfolio can easily beat the market over time. That is, if the individual holdings are all above average or excellent quality.

Bottom Line: Even The Best Strategies Don't Work All The Time So Patience, Perseverance And Discipline Are Essential To Achieving Your Financial Dreams It's easy to fall into the trap of obsessing over short-term stock price movements, and thinking that any strategy that doesn't outperform the market all the time is a failure.
However, Warren Buffett's success (and decades of market studies) shows that this is a flawed way of thinking. Ultimately, the trick to becoming prosperous and achieving your financial goals means knowing the right strategies to use that fit your needs. But it also requires having the patience, discipline, and perseverance to wait for your long-term strategy to play out and make you rich over time.
